title: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks
summary: This memo discusses congestion control in IP and TCP networks, including how many tiny packets can bog down a network, and makes suggestions for better behavior. It is a discussion paper that does not specify a standard. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805.

eli5.summary: If everyone sends a tiny envelope for each word, the mail truck jams. This note suggests waiting a moment and sending several words together.

subtitle: John Nagle's 1984 note on congestion collapse, the small-packet fix that became the Nagle algorithm, and ICMP Source Quench handling.

tldr.problem: IP gateways joining networks of very different bandwidth can fall into congestion collapse, and tiny TCP packets add heavy overhead on loaded networks.
tldr.mechanism: TCP holds back new segments while earlier data is unacknowledged, and reacts to ICMP Source Quench by acting as if the window were zero until 10 ACKs arrive. Gateways are urged to send quenches early and to discard fairly.
tldr.outcome: The memo specifies no standard, and it is Historic and obsoleted by RFC 7805.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This memo discusses congestion control in IP/TCP internetworks. It is meant to stimulate thought and discussion; it makes some specific suggestions but does not specify any standards.

The author reports that IP, a pure datagram protocol, and TCP, used together, suffer unusual congestion problems from interactions between the transport and datagram layers. Gateways are vulnerable to what he calls congestion collapse, especially where they connect networks of widely different bandwidth. The problem is not widely recognized because most use is on ARPANET IMP based networks, which have uniform bandwidth and substantial excess capacity.

The experience comes from Ford Aerospace and Ford Motor Company's private IP/TCP network, where link bandwidth varies from 1200 to 10,000,000 bits per second and transit times of several seconds are common.
sections.eli5: A truck driver explains why roads jam when lots of small cars and one narrow bridge meet. Nobody has to follow his advice yet; he wants people to think about it.

sections.title: Congestion Collapse
sections.content:
In a heavily loaded pure datagram network with end to end retransmission, congestion raises round-trip time and the number of datagrams in transit. This is normal while only one copy of each datagram is in transit. Trouble starts when retransmission of undelivered datagrams begins.

A sudden load, such as a new bulk file transfer filling a large window, can make round-trip time rise faster than hosts can update their measurements. Once it exceeds a host's maximum retransmission interval, that host adds more copies of the same datagrams. Switching node buffers fill, packets are dropped, and every packet is sent several times.

The condition is stable: with fair dropping the network keeps running in a degraded state, with throughput a small fraction of normal. Adding gateway memory does not fix it, because it only delays the onset and makes the eventual collapse worse, with more duplicates. A few badly behaved hosts can congest gateways and block other hosts.
sections.eli5: When the line is slow, impatient kids keep repeating their question, which makes the line even slower. Soon everyone is repeating and nothing gets through.

sections.title: The Small-Packet Problem and Its Fix
sections.content:
When TCP carries single keystrokes, each byte of data travels in a 41 byte packet (one byte of data, 40 bytes of header), a 4000% overhead. This is tolerable on a lightly loaded network but can cause lost datagrams and aborted connections on a heavy one. The older remedy, from Tymnet in the late 1960s, delayed small packets for a short time (200-500ms). Its flaw is that no single time limit suits both a 10M bit per second Ethernet and a heavily loaded net with a five second round-trip time.

The proposed solution is to inhibit sending new TCP segments when new data arrives from the user if any previously transmitted data on the connection remains unacknowledged. It is unconditional: no timers or size tests are needed, and implementation typically takes one or two lines. Deferred data is sent when an ACK or a window update arrives, an idle connection sends at once, and normal retransmission is untouched.

In the five second round-trip example, 25 packets would otherwise be sent in 5 seconds. With this scheme the first character goes at once and the next 24 go in one packet when the ACK returns, cutting overhead to 320%, a factor of 4.7 better than the timer scheme. For file transfers the cost is a startup delay: 254 seconds instead of 250 seconds for a 100K byte file in the author's example, a difference of 1.6%. The memo concludes the scheme gives at least 98% of the performance of the other approaches in every case examined.
sections.eli5: Do not mail a new envelope until the last one is confirmed delivered. Meanwhile, keep adding words to the next envelope so it leaves full.

sections.title: Congestion Control with ICMP Source Quench
sections.content:
Because the author's network has no node-to-node flow control, the only mechanism under the IP standard is the ICMP Source Quench message. The memo argues gateways should send it before buffers run out; the author's experience is about when half the buffering space is exhausted, a reasonable engineering decision rather than the result of extensive experimentation. Waiting until packets are dropped is called wasteful and open to congestion collapse.

On the host side, the author's first implementation made TCP act as if the window size were zero whenever the window was not empty after a Source Quench, until 10 ACKs had been received. A similar but more elaborate throttle was built by David Mills. Source Quench does not inhibit acknowledgements or retransmissions, since holding those back causes unnecessary traffic or lost connections. Connections stay alive at reduced bandwidth.

Other protocols at the same layer should also respond. The only serious problem noted is the User Datagram Protocol, and the author had not implemented throttling in those protocols.
sections.eli5: The gateway shouts slow down before the room is full. The sender then sends one small piece at a time until ten replies come back, but still answers and repeats when it has to.

sections.title: Gateway Self-Defense and Conclusion
sections.content:
Gateways are vulnerable to host mismanagement of congestion. In late 1983 a TCP bug in an ARPANET host sent retransmissions of the same datagram as fast as the ARPANET would accept them, ignoring Source Quench messages and effectively disconnecting the author's network for several hours until the host crashed.

The memo suggests that future gateways defend themselves. One idea is to discard the latest packet from the host that has the most packets queued, which tends to balance throughput among hosts; the author had not tried it yet. Another is to discard a newly arrived packet that duplicates one already queued, using hashing; this helps against poor retransmission control but not malicious hosts. A host that ignores Source Quench could be disconnected, though detecting that is non-trivial and left as research.

The conclusion is that effective solutions exist, and TCP implementations must address several key issues in ways at least as effective as those described if IP/TCP networks are to run under heavy load.
sections.eli5: If one kid keeps shouting and ignores the teacher, the gateway may skip his extra copies or stop listening to him so the other kids can still talk.
